The Great Barrier Reef is one of the richest and most complex natural systems in the world. The Reef's diverse range of habitats all connect and support each other, which means they are all vital to the life of the Great Barrier Reef.

Assertion : A larger dry cell has higher emf. 
Reason : The emf of a dry cell is proportional to its size.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion
If assertion is true but reason is false
If both assertion and reason are false.
1345.sol: The electrical force of a cell or battery called electromotive force (emf). This force, which makes electrons flow around a circuit. Each kind of cell has a particular emf. The size of a cell has no effect on its emf. The chemicals in the cell determines its emf, but large cells last longer than small cells of same basic type. This means that from a large cell, we get a particular em $\mathrm{f}$ for more time as compared to small cell.

1890.text: Plasmid vector in DNA recombinant technology means
options: a virus that transfers gene to bacteria
any fragment of DNA carrying desirable gene.
1890.sol: The vectors are DNA molecules that can carry a foreign DNA segment and replicate inside the host cell. Plasmid vectors are extra-chromosomal, self-replicating, usually circular, double-stranded DNA molecules, found naturally in many bacteria and also in some yeast. Although plasmids are usually not essential for normal cell growth and division, they often confer some traits to the host organisms, for example, resistance to certain antibiotics or toxins that can be a selective advantage under certain conditions. These naturally occurring plasmids have been modified to serve as vectors in the laboratory.

Observe the following statements regarding \($\mathrm{C}_{60}$\).
i. All carbons are \(s p²\)-hybridised.
ii. It contains 12 rings of five carbons each and 20 rings of six carbons each.

4566.sol:
In \($\mathrm{C}_{60}$\), all carbon atoms are \(s p²\)-hybridised. It contains 12 rings of five carbon each and 20 rings of six carbon each. It is prepared by heating graphite in an electric arc under inert condition (He gas).
Thus, statements (i), (ii), (iv) and (v) are correct.

5734.subject: Chemistry
5734.text: An electron is moving in Bohr's fourth orbit. Its de-Broglie wave length is $\lambda$. What is the circumference of the fourth orbit?
5734.sol:
According to Bohr's concept, an electron always move in the orbit with angular momentum (m v r)$ equal to $n h / 2 \pi$.
\therefore \quad m v r=\frac{n h}{2 \pi}$
or
$r=\frac{n}{2 \pi} \cdot\left(\frac{h}{m v}\right) \text{ or } r=\frac{n \lambda}{2 \pi}$
(From de -Broglie equation, $\lambda=\frac{h}{m v}$ )
for fourth orbit $n=4\begin{gathered}
r=\frac{2 \lambda}{\pi} \\
\therefore \text{ circumference }=2 \pi r=2 \pi \times \frac{2 \lambda}{\pi}=4 \lambda
\end{gathered}$

5967.text: At $60 ° C$, dinitrogen tetroxide is fifty percent dissociated. Find its standard free energy change at this temperature and one atmosphere. [ Given: $log1. 33 = 0. 1239$& ]

The reaction showing the dissociation will be:

$\begin{cases} & {N}_{2}{O}_{4} ( s ) & ⇌ & 2{NO}_{2} ( g ) \\ t = 0 & 1mol & & 0mol \\ t = {t}_{eq} & 0 . 5mol & & 1mol\end{cases}$

Clearly, from this equation we can say that the total number of moles is& $

$0 . 5 + 1 = 1 . 5mol$

Hence, the partial pressure for the molecule will be$

${P}_{{N}_{2}{O}_{4}} = \dfrac{0 . 5}{1 . 5} \times 1atm = \dfrac{1}{3}atm{P}_{NO2} = \dfrac{1}{1 . 5} \times 1atm = \dfrac{2}{3}atm$

Now, according to the law of chemical equilibrium we know that $

${K}_{sp} = $\dfrac{P^{2}{NO}_{2}}{P{N}_{2}{O}_{4}} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)2}{\dfrac{1}{3}} =$1 . 33atm$

We know that at equilibrium the free Gibb's energy is: $

$∆ G = - 2 . 303 \times RT \times \left(\log_{10}{K}_{P}\right) ∆ G = - 2 . 303 \times \left(8 . 314{JK}^{- 1}{mol}^{- 1}\right) \times \left(333K\right) \times \left[\log_{10}\left(1 . 33\right)\right] ∆ G = - 790{Jmol}^{- 1}$

6636.text:
The sum of all the coefficients in the binomial expansion of \((1+2 x)^n\) is 6561. Let \(R=(I+2 x)^n=I+F\), where \(I \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(0 < F < \mathrm{l}\).
If \$x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, then \$1-\frac{F}{1+(\sqrt{2}-1)^4}=$
6636.sol:
It is given that sum of all the coefficients in the binomial expansion of \((1+2 x)^n\) is \(6561=(1+2)^n\) on putting \(x=1\).
\$(\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow$& 3^n=6561 \\
\Rightarrow & n=8
\end{array}\)
Now, at \(x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$\), then \(R=(1+2 x)^n=I+F\)
\$(\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow R=(\sqrt{2}+$1)^8=I+F, $\text{ where }$ I \in \mathbb{N} $\text{ and }$0  <  F <  1 \\
& \therefore(\sqrt{2}-$1)^8=F^{\prime}, \text{ where }$0 <  F^{\prime} <  1 \\
& \therefore(\sqrt{2}+$1)^8+(\sqrt{2}-$1)^8=I+$\left(F+F^{\prime}\right)\\
& \Rightarrow 2\left[(\sqrt{2})^$8+{ }^8 C_2(\sqrt{2})^$6+{ }^8 C_4(\sqrt{2})^$4+{ }^8 C_6(\sqrt{2})^$2+{ }^8 C_8\right] \\
& \quad=I+\left(F+F^{\prime}\right)\\
& \Rightarrow \text{ Even integer }=$ I+$\left(F+F^{\prime}\right)\\
& \Rightarrow F+F^{\prime} \in \text{ Integer }\\
& \because 0 <  F <  1 \text{ and }$0 <  F^{\prime} <  1 \Rightarrow 0 <  F+F^{\prime} <  2 \\
 $\text{ So, }$ F+F^{\prime}=1 \\
& \Rightarrow F=1-F^{\prime}=1-(\sqrt{2}-$1)^8
\end{aligned}\)
\$(\begin{aligned}$ \text{ So, }$1-\frac{F}{1+(\sqrt{2}-1)^4}=$1-\frac{1-(\sqrt{2}-1)^8}{1+(\sqrt{2}-1)^4}\\
& =1-\frac{\left[1+(\sqrt{2}-1)^4\right]\left[1-(\sqrt{2}-1)^4\right]}{1+(\sqrt{2}-1)^4}\\
& =1-\left[1-(\sqrt{2}-$1)^4\right]=(\sqrt{2}-$1)^4
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (3) is correct.

8132.text: $y = Ae^{x} + Be^{- 2x}$ satisfies which of the following differential equations?
8132.sol:
$y = Ae^{x} + Be^{- 2x}$

On differentiating, we get

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = Ae^{x} - 2Be^{- 2x}$

Subtracting both the above equations, we get

8172.subject: Mathematics
8172.text:
Statement (I) The elimination of arbitrary constants from \(\alpha, \beta\) and \(\gamma\) from \(y=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma) x\) results in a differential equation of order three.
Statement (II) The elimination of arbitrary constants \(\alpha, \beta\) and \(\gamma\) from \(y=\alpha x+\beta \sin x+\gamma e^x\) results in a differential equation of order three.
options: I is true and II is false
I is false and II is false
I is true and II is true
I is false and II is true
8172.sol:
Statement I
\(\Rightarrow \quad y=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)x\)
Differentiate both sides w.r.t. \(x\), we get
\(\frac{d y}{d x}=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=k\)
Here, order \(=1\)
So, statement \(\mathrm{I}\) is false.
Statements II : \(y=\alpha x+\beta \sin x+\gamma e^x\)
Differentiate both sides w.r.t. \(x\), we get
\(\frac{d y}{d x}=\alpha+\beta \cosx+\gamma e^x\)...(i)
Again, differentiating both sides w. r. t. \(x\), we get
\(\Rightarrow \quad \begin{aligned}\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}& =-\beta \sin x+\gamma e^x \quad \ldots (ii) \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d^3 y}{d x^2}& =-\beta \cos x+\gamma e^x \quad \ldots (iii)
\end{aligned}\)
Subtracting Eq. (ii) from Eq. (iii), we get
\begin{aligned}$\frac{d^3 y}{d x²}-\frac{d^2 y}{d x²}$& =-\beta $\cos x+\gamma$ e^x+\beta $\sin x-\gamma$ e^x \\
& =\beta $\sin x-\beta \cos x$ \\
& =\beta($\sin x-\cos$ x)
\end{aligned}
Hence, order \(=3\)
So, statement II is true.

9848.text: If $A$ is a matrix $\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{array}\right]$, then $A^n=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ n & 1\end{array}\right]$, $\forall n \in N$
9848.sol:
Given, If $A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{array}\right]$, then $A^n=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ n & 1\end{array}\right], \forall n \in N$
We will generalise the exponent of $A$.
Let $n=2$
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore$A² & =$\left[\begin{array}{ll}$1 & 0 \\
1 & 1
\end{array}\right] $\cdot\left[\begin{array}{ll}$1 & 0 \\
1 & 1
\end{array}\right] \\
& =$\left[\begin{array}{cc}$1 $\cdot$1+0 $\cdot$1 & 1 $\cdot$0+0 $\cdot$1 \\
1 $\cdot$1+1 $\cdot$1 & 1 $\cdot$0+1 $\cdot$1
\end{array}\right]=$\left[\begin{array}{ll}$1 & 0 \\
2 & 1
\end{array}\right]
\end{aligned}

Again, let $n=3$
\therefore A³=A² $\cdot$A=$\left[\begin{array}{ll}$1 & 0 \\
2 & 1
\end{array}\right] $\cdot\left[\begin{array}{ll}$1 & 0 \\
1 & 1
\end{array}\right]=$\left[\begin{array}{cc}$1 & 0 \\
2+1 & 1
\end{array}\right]=$\left[\begin{array}{ll}$1 & 0 \\
3 & 1
\end{array}\right]

Similarly, $A^4=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{array}\right]$
Hence, $A^n=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ n & 1\end{array}\right]$ is true for $n=3$

& \Rightarrow 1-P(A \cup B)=\frac{1}{3} \\
& \Rightarrow P(A \cup B)=\frac{2}{3} \\
& \Rightarrow P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)=\frac{2}{3} \\
& \Rightarrow x+y-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{2}{3} \Rightarrow x+y=\frac{5}{6}
\end{aligned}$
Now, $x\left(\frac{5}{6}-x\right)=\frac{1}{6} \Rightarrow 5 x-6 x^2=1\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow 6 x^2-5 x+1=0 \\
& \Rightarrow(2 x-1)(3 x-1)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{2} \text{$ or $} \frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow P(A)=\frac{1}{2} \text{ or } \frac{1}{3}
\end{aligned}$

10692.text: Two persons $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{Q}$ are considering to apply for a job. The probability that $\mathrm{P}$ applies for the job is $1 / 4$, the probability that $\mathrm{P}$ applies for the job given that $\mathrm{Q}$ applies for the job is $1 / 2$, and the probability that $Q$ applies for the job given that $P$ applies for the job is $1 / 3$. & $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{P} \cap \mathrm{Q})=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{12}
\end{aligned}$ So, $\frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{P} \cap \mathrm{Q})}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{Q})}=\frac{1}{2} \begin{aligned}$& P(Q)=2 $\times \frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{6}$\\
& P(\bar{Q})=1-P(Q)=1-$\frac{1}{6}=\frac{5}{6}$\\
& P(\bar{P})=1-P(P)=1-$\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{4}$\\
& P(\bar{P} \cup \bar{Q})=1-P(P \cap Q) \\
& =1-$\frac{1}{12}=\frac{11}{12}
\end{aligned}$ Then, $\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{P}} \cap \overline{\mathrm{Q}})=\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{P}})+\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{Q}})-\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{P}} \cup \overline{\mathrm{Q}}) \begin{aligned}$& =$\frac{3}{4}+\frac{5}{6}-\frac{11}{12}$\\
& =$\frac{18+20-22}{24}=\frac{38-22}{24}=\frac{16}{24}=\frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}$ Now, $\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\overline{\mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{Q}}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{P}} \cap \overline{\mathrm{Q}})}{\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{Q}})}$
=$\frac{\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{5}{6}}=\frac{4}{5}$

10807.text: From a group of 50 students, two sections comprising of 20 and 30 students are formed. If Ram and Rahim are two particular students among the 50 students, then the probability that they both belong to the same section is
10807.sol:
Total number of students \(=50\)
Number of ways of making groups if both the students are in first group \(=\binom{48}{18} \times\binom{30}{30}=\binom{48}{18}\) and number of ways of making groups if both the students are in second group
\(=\binom{48}{28} \times\binom{20}{20}=\binom{48}{28}\)
and total number of ways \(=\binom{50}{20} \times\binom{30}{30}=\binom{50}{20}\)
\(\begin{gathered}
\therefore \text{ Required probability }=\frac{\binom{48}{18}+\binom{48}{28}}{\binom{50}{20}}\\
=\frac{\frac{48 !}{18 ! 30 !}+\frac{48 !}{28 ! 20 !}}{\frac{50 !}{20 ! 30 !}}\\
=\frac{\frac{1}{30 \times 29}+\frac{1}{20 \times 19}}{\frac{50 \times 49}{20 \times 19 \times 30 \times 29}}=\frac{(20 \times 19)+(30 \times 29)}{(50 \times 49)}\\
=\frac{38+87}{5 \times 49}=\frac{125}{5 \times 49}=\frac{25}{49}
\end{gathered}\)
Hence, option (a) is correct.

15286.text: A deflection magnetometer is adjusted and a magnet of magnetic moment $M$ is placed on it in the usual manner and the observed deflection is $\theta$. The period of oscillation of the needle before settling of the deflection is $T$. When the magnet is removed, the period of oscillation of the needle is $T_0$ before settling to $0^{{}^{\circ}}-0^{{}^{\circ}}$. If the earth's induced magnetic field is $B_H$, the relation between $T$ and $T_0$ is
15286.sol:
In deflection magnetometer, field due to magnet $F$ and horizontal component $B_H$ of earth's field are perpendicular to each other.
$\therefore$ Net field is $\sqrt{F^2+B_H^2}$
So the time period
$T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{1}{M \sqrt{F^2+B_H}}}$
When magnet is removed
$T_0=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{1}{M B_H}}$
Also, $\quad \frac{F}{B_H}=\tan \theta$
Dividing Eqs. (i) by (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned} \frac{T}{T_0} & =\sqrt{\frac{B_H}{\sqrt{F^2+B_H^2}}} \\ & =\sqrt{\frac{B_H}{\sqrt{B_H^2+\tan ^2 \theta+B_H^2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{B_H}{B_H \sqrt{\sec ^2 \theta}}} \\ & =\sqrt{\cos \theta} \\ \Rightarrow \quad T^2 & =T_0^2 \cos \theta\end{aligned}$

$⇒ cos\left(\omegat\right) = - \dfrac{1}{2} = cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

19614.subject: Chemistry
19614.text: An organic compound with molecular formula $\mathrm{C}_3 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{N}$ on hydrolysis gives compound '$\mathrm{X}$' which on treatment with $\mathrm{Cl}_2 / \mathrm{P}$ gives compound '$\mathrm{Y}$'. Compound '$\mathrm{Y}$' on reaction with $\mathrm{NH}_3$ gives '$\mathrm{Z}$'. The compound '$\mathrm{Z}$' is :
19614.sol:
The molecular formula $\mathrm{C}_3 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{N}$ corresponds to propionitrile ($\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{CN}$).

Hydrolysis of propionitrile ($\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{CN} + 2\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{COOH} + \mathrm{NH}_3$) yields propanoic acid as compound '$\mathrm{X}$'.

Treatment of propanoic acid with $\mathrm{Cl}_2 / \mathrm{P}$ is the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction, which results in $\alpha$-chlorination: $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{COOH} + \mathrm{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathrm{P}} \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CHClCOOH}$ (2-chloropropanoic acid) as compound '$\mathrm{Y}$'.

Reaction of 2-chloropropanoic acid with $\mathrm{NH}_3$ involves nucleophilic substitution of the chlorine atom by the amino group: $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CHClCOOH} + 2\mathrm{NH}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{NH}_2)\mathrm{COOH} + \mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{Cl}$.

The product '$\mathrm{Z}$' is 2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine).

Answer: 2-aminopropanoic acid

19628.text: Rank the following compounds in order of increasing basicity.
19628.sol:
Compound 1: Aniline (C_6H_5NH_2$) - lone pair on N delocalised into ring via resonance \to moderate basicity.

Compound 2: Benzylamine (C_6H_5CH_2NH_2$) - $NH_2$ not directly attached to ring, no resonance with ring \to most basic among these.

Compound 3: 2-Nitroaniline - $-NO_2$ at ortho position withdraws electrons by both inductive and resonance effects, plus steric hindrance prevents coplanarity reducing basicity further \to less basic than aniline.

Compound 4: Benzamide (C_6H_5CONH_2$) - lone pair on N delocalised into $C=O$ (amide resonance), making N least basic.

Increasing basicity: 4 < 3 < 1 < 2$. Answer: (2)

20676.subject: Chemistry
20676.text: The system that forms maximum boiling azeotropes is
20676.sol:
Azeotropes are mixtures of liquids that boil at a constant temperature and possess the same composition in the liquid and vapor phases. Azeotropes are classified into two types based on their deviation from Raoult's Law.

Minimum boiling azeotropes are formed by solutions showing large positive deviations from Raoult's Law. Examples include ethyl alcohol-water and $\mathrm{CS}_2+$ acetone.

Maximum boiling azeotropes are formed by solutions showing large negative deviations from Raoult's Law. In these cases, the intermolecular forces between the components are stronger than the forces between the pure components, leading to a decrease in vapor pressure and an increase in the boiling point.

The mixture of acetone and chloroform exhibits strong hydrogen bonding between the oxygen atom of acetone and the hydrogen atom of chloroform, resulting in a large negative deviation from Raoult's Law. Therefore, the acetone-chloroform system forms a maximum boiling azeotrope.

Answer: acetone-chloroform

21002.subject: Mathematics
21002.text: If the area of region bounded by the lines $y=2 x+1, x$-axis, $x=a$ and $x=3$ is 10 sq units. Then the value of ' $a$ ' is
21002.sol:
The area $A$ of the region bounded by the line $y = 2x + 1$, the $x$-axis, $x = a$, and $x = 3$ is given by the definite integral of the function $f(x) = 2x + 1$ from $a$ to $3$.

$A = \int_a^{3} (2x + 1) dx = 10$

Evaluating the integral:

$[x^2 + x]_a^{3} = 10$

Substituting the limits:

$(3^2 + 3) - (a^2 + a) = 10$

$(9 + 3) - (a^2 + a) = 10$

$12 - a^2 - a = 10$

$a^2 + a - 2 = 0$

Factoring the quadratic equation:

$(a + 2)(a - 1) = 0$

The possible values for $a$ are $a = 1$ or $a = -2$. Since the region is bounded between $x = a$ and $x = 3$, and the line $y = 2x + 1$ intersects the $x$-axis at $x = -0.5$, we consider the positive value $a = 1$.

Answer: 1

21617.subject: Mathematics
21617.sol:
The expression for $\alpha$ is given by $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(\tan \dfrac{5\pi}{4})$. Since $\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$ is in the third quadrant, $\tan \dfrac{5\pi}{4} = \tan(\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4}) = \tan \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$.

Thus, $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

The expression for $\beta$ is given by $\beta = \tan^{-1}(-\tan \dfrac{2\pi}{3})$. Since $\tan \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \tan(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}) = -\tan \dfrac{\pi}{3} = -\sqrt{3}$, we have $-\tan \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}$.

Thus, $\beta = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3}) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Checking the options:

Option (1): $\alpha + \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \neq -\dfrac{7\pi}{12}$.

Option (2): $3\alpha = 3(\dfrac{\pi}{4}) = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ and $4\beta = 4(\dfrac{\pi}{3}) = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$. These are not equal.

Option (3): $\alpha - \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{\pi}{12} \neq \dfrac{7\pi}{12}$.

Option (4): $4\alpha = 4(\dfrac{\pi}{4}) = \pi$ and $3\beta = 3(\dfrac{\pi}{3}) = \pi$. Since $4\alpha = 3\beta = \pi$, this option is correct.

Answer: $4 \alpha=3 \beta$

21662.subject: Mathematics
21662.sol:
The given limit is $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a^x - b^x}{x}$.

Rewrite the expression by adding and subtracting $1$ in the numerator:

$\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{(a^x - 1) - (b^x - 1)}{x}$

Using the property of limits, this can be split into two separate limits:

$\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{a^x - 1}{x} - \lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{b^x - 1}{x}$

Recall the standard limit formula $\lim_{x \rightarrow 0} \dfrac{k^x - 1}{x} = \ln k$.

Applying this formula to both terms:

$\ln a - \ln b$

Using the logarithmic property $\ln a - \ln b = \ln \left( \dfrac{a}{b} \right),$ the result is $\log \left( \dfrac{a}{b} \right).

Answer: \log \dfrac{a}{b}$

21910.subject: Mathematics
21910.text: Let $\mathrm{A}$ and ${B}$ be two events such that $P(A / B)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(B / A)=\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $P(A \cap B)=\dfrac{1}{6}$ then, which one of the following is not true?
21910.sol:
Given $P(A|B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{6}$, we have $\dfrac{1/6}{P(B)} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, which implies $P(B) = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

Given $P(B|A) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{6}$, we have $\dfrac{1/6}{P(A)} = \dfrac{1}{3}$, which implies $P(A) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Check for independence: $P(A) \times P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{6}$. Since $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{6}$, we have $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$, so $A$ and $B$ are independent events.

Evaluate $P(A' \cap B) = P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{6}$. This is true.

Evaluate $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{3+2-1}{6} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$. This is true.

Since $A$ and $B$ are independent, the statement that $A$ and $B$ are not independent is false.

Answer: $\mathrm{A} \text{ and } \mathrm{B} \text{ are not independent }$

22733.subject: Physics
22733.text: Around the central part of an air cored solenoid of length $20 \mathrm{ cm}$ and area of cross section $1.4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}^2$ and 3000 turns, another coil of 250 turns is closely wound. A current $2 \mathrm{ A}$ in the solenoid is reversed in $0.2 \mathrm{ s}$, then the induced emf produced is
22733.sol:
The magnetic field $B$ inside a long solenoid is given by $B = \mu_{0} n I$, where $n = \dfrac{N}{l}$ is the number of turns per unit length.

Given: $N_{1} = 3000$, $l = 0.2 \text{ m}$, $I_{initial} = 2 \text{ A}$, $I_{final} = -2 \text{ A}$, $A = 1.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^2$, $N_{2} = 250$, $\Delta t = 0.2 \text{ s}$.

The magnetic flux $\phi$ through the secondary coil is $\phi = B A = \mu_{0} \left( \dfrac{N_{1}}{l} \right) I A$.

The change in magnetic flux $\Delta \phi$ is $\Delta \phi = \phi_{final} - \phi_{initial} = \mu_{0} \left( \dfrac{N_{1}}{l} \right) A (I_{final} - I_{initial})$.

Substituting the values:
$\Delta \phi = (4 \pi \times 10^{-7}) \times \left( \dfrac{3000}{0.2} \right) \times (1.4 \times 10^{-3}) \times (-2 - 2)$
$\Delta \phi = (4 \pi \times 10^{-7}) \times (15000) \times (1.4 \times 10^{-3}) \times (-4)$
$\Delta \phi = -1.055 \times 10^{-4} \text{ Wb}$ (approx).

The induced emf $\varepsilon$ in the secondary coil is given by Faraday's law: $\varepsilon = -N_{2} \dfrac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t}$.

$\varepsilon = -250 \times \dfrac{-1.055 \times 10^{-4}}{0.2} = 1250 \times 1.055 \times 10^{-4} = 0.131875 \text{ V}$.

Rounding to the nearest value, $\varepsilon \approx 1.32 \times 10^{-1} \text{ V}$.

Answer: $1.32 \times 10^{-1} \mathrm{ V}$

22787.subject: Physics
22787.text: A charge of $5\ \mu C$ is placed at the centre of a spherical shell $S_1$ of radius 10 cm. Now this system is enclosed inside another spherical shell $S_2$ of radius 20 cm. The ratio of the electrical flux through the surface $S_2$ to $S_1$ is :
22787.sol:
According to Gauss's law, the total electric flux through a closed surface depends only on the net charge enclosed by the surface, given by $\Phi = \dfrac{q_{enclosed}}{\varepsilon_0}$.

For the spherical shell $S_1$, the enclosed charge is $q = 5\ \mu C$.

$\Phi_1 = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$

For the spherical shell $S_2$, which encloses $S_1$ and the charge, the total enclosed charge is also $q = 5\ \mu C$.

$\Phi_2 = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$

The ratio of the electrical flux through $S_2$ to $S_1$ is:

$\dfrac{\Phi_2}{\Phi_1} = \dfrac{q / \varepsilon_0}{q / \varepsilon_0} = 1$

The ratio is $1:1$.

Answer: $1:1$

23728.text: If frequencies are $(v-1)$ and $(v+2)$, then find the value of beats.
23728.sol:
The beat frequency is defined as the absolute difference between the two given frequencies.

Given frequencies are $f_1 = v - 1$ and $f_2 = v + 2$.

Beat frequency = $|f_2 - f_1|$

Beat frequency = $|(v + 2) - (v - 1)|$

Beat frequency = $|v + 2 - v + 1|$

Beat frequency = $|3| = 3$.

Answer: 3

25148.text: The correct statement(s) pertaining to the adsorption of a gas on a solid surface is(are)
options:
Adsorption is always exothermic

Physisorption may transform into chemisorption at high temperature

Physisorption increases with increasing temperature but chemisorption decreases with increasing temperature

Chemisorption is more exothermic than physisorption, however it is very slow due to higher energy of activation
25148.sol:
(a) In the process of adsorption, a bond is formed between adsorbate and adsorbent, hence always exothermic.
(b) Physisorption require very low activation energy while chemisorption require high activation energy. Therefore a physisorption may transform into chemisorption but only at high temperature.
(c) It is wrong statement as at higher temperature, physically adsorbed substance starts desorbing.
(d) In physical adsorption, van der Waals' force hold the adsorbate and adsorbent together which is a weak electrostatic attraction. In chemisorption, strong chemical bond binds the adsorbate to the adsorbent. Therefore, chemisorption is more exothermic than physical adsorption.

28149.subject: Chemistry
28149.text:
Observe the following reactions at $\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{K})$.
I. $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow$ products.
II. $5 \mathrm{Br}^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+\mathrm{BrO}_{3}{ }^{-}(\mathrm{aq})+6 \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{Br}_{2}(\mathrm{aq})+3 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})$
Both the reactions are started at 10.00 am. The rates of these reactions at 10.10 am are same. The value of $-\frac{\Delta\left[\mathrm{Br}^{-}\right]}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}$ at 10.10 am is $2 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~min}^{-1}$. The concentration of A at 10.10 am is $10^{-2} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$. What is the first order rate constant (in $\mathrm{min}^{-1}$) of reaction $I$ ?
28149.sol:
For reaction II:
5Br$^-$ + BrO$_3^-$ + 6H$^+$ $\rightarrow$ 3Br$_2$ + 3H$_2$O,
The overall reaction rate is:
$r = -\frac{1}{5}\frac{\Delta[Br^-]}{\Delta t} = -\frac{1}{3}\frac{\Delta[Br_2]}{\Delta t}$.
Given $\frac{\Delta[Br^-]}{\Delta t} = 2 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ min$^{-1}$
The reaction rate is $r = \frac{2 \times 10^{-4}}{5} = 4 \times 10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$ min$^{-1}$.
Since the rates of both reactions are equal at 10.10 am and reaction I is first-order:
$r = k[A]$, so $4 \times 10^{-5} = k \times 10^{-2}$, giving $k = 4 \times 10^{-3}$ min$^{-1}$.

gm equivalent of remaining ${H}_{2}{SO}_{4} = 12 - 2 = 10$

32839.text: Let the quadratic curve passing through the point $\left(- 1, 0\right)$ and touching the line $y = x$ at $\left(1, 1\right)$ be $y = f \left(x\right). Then$ the x-intercept of $the normal to the curve at the point \left(\alpha, \alpha + 1\right) in the first quadrant is$
32839.sol:
Given,

The quadratic curve passing through the point $\left(- 1, 0\right)$ and touching the line $y = x$ at $\left(1, 1\right)$ be $y = f\left(x\right)$,

Now let the curve be $y = a{x}^{2} + bx + c$

Passes through $\left(- 1, 0\right)$

$⇒ a - b + c = 0 . . . . \left(i\right)$

Passes through $\left(1, 1\right)$

$⇒ a + b + c = 1 . . . . . \ldots \left(ii\right)$

Now given tangent to $y = x$ at $\left(1, 1\right)$,

So, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$

$⇒ 2a + b = 1 . . . . \ldots \left(iii\right)$

Solving all above three equations we get,

$a = \dfrac{1}{4}, b = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $c = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Hence, the equation of curve is $y = \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{4} + \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4}$

Now $\left(\alpha, \alpha + 1\right)$ lies on curve

$\alpha +1= \dfrac{{\alpha}^{2}}{4} + \dfrac{\alpha}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4}$

$⇒ ( \alpha - 3 ) ( \alpha + 1 ) = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = 3$
Point in first quadrant is $\left(3, 4\right)$

Now finding slope of tangent at $\left(3, 4\right)$ we get,

${\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}_{\left(3, 4\right)} = {\left(\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)}_{\left(3, 4\right)} = 2$

$⇒$ Slope of normal $= \dfrac{- 1}{2}$

Hence, equation of normal will be, $y - 4 = - \dfrac{1}{2} ( x - 3 )$

So, $x$- intercept $= 11$

33633.text: Let the abscissae of the two points $P$ and $Q$ be the roots of $2{x}^{2} - rx + p = 0$ and the ordinates of $P$ and $Q$ be the roots of ${x}^{2} - sx - q = 0$. If the equation of the circle described on $PQ$ as diameter is $2\left({x}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right) - 11x - 14y - 22 = 0$, then $2r + s - 2q + p$ is equal to ______.
33633.sol:
Let the roots of $2{x}^{2} - rx + p = 0$ are ${x}_{1}, {x}_{2}$ and roots of ${y}^{2} - sy - q = 0$ are ${y}_{1}, {y}_{2}$

So, ${x}_{1} + {x}_{2} = \dfrac{r}{2}, {x}_{1}{x}_{2} = \dfrac{p}{2}, {y}_{1} + {y}_{2} = s, {y}_{1}{y}_{2} = - q$

Equation of the circle with $PQ$ as diameter will be

$\left(x - {x}_{1}\right)\left(x - {x}_{2}\right) + \left(y - {y}_{1}\right)\left(y - {y}_{2}\right) = 0$

i.e. $2\left({x}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right) - rx - 2sy + p - 2q = 0$

On comparing with the given equation $r = 11, s = 7$

$p - 2q = - 22$

$∴ 2r + s - 2q + p = 22 + 7 - 22 = 7$

34199.text: If ${∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\sqrt{1 - sin2x}dx = \alpha + \beta\sqrt{2} + \gamma\sqrt{3}$, where $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are rational numbers, then $3\alpha + 4\beta - \gamma$ is equal to _____.
34199.sol:
Given,

${∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\sqrt{1 - sin2x}dx = \alpha + \beta\sqrt{2} + \gamma\sqrt{3}$

Now, let $I = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\sqrt{1 - sin2x}dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} | sinx - cosx | dx$

$⇒ I = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} ( cosx - sinx ) dx + {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} ( sinx - cosx ) dx$

$⇒ I = - 1 + 2\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3}$

Now, comparing with 

$I = \alpha + \beta\sqrt{2} + \gamma\sqrt{3}$

We get, $\alpha = - 1, \beta = 2, \gamma = - 1$

Hence, $3\alpha + 4\beta - \gamma = - 3 + 8 + 1 = 6$

34999.sol:

$⇒ 5\left(\alpha\right) + 7\left(0\right) = 50, 5\left(0\right) + 7\left(\beta\right) = 50$

$⇒ \alpha = 10, \beta = \dfrac{50}{7}$

Also, $P$ divide the line segment $AB$ internally in the ratio $7: 3$.

$⇒ P ≡ \left(\dfrac{7 \times 0 + 3 \times 10}{7 + 3}, \dfrac{7 \times \dfrac{50}{7} + 3 \times 0}{7 + 3}\right)$

$⇒ P ≡ \left(3, 5\right)$

$⇒ ae = 3$ as perpendicular from $S$ passes through $P$

Now, $3x - 25 = 0$ is a directrix of the ellipse $E: \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{25}{3}$

We know that, directrix of an ellipse is given by $x = \pm \dfrac{a}{e}$

$⇒ \dfrac{a}{e} = \dfrac{25}{3}$

Also, $ae = 3$

$⇒ a = 5, b = 4$

Length of LR $= \dfrac{2{b}^{2}}{a} = \dfrac{32}{5}$

35176.text: Let $A = \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\right\}$ and $B = \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}$. Then the number of functions $f: A \to B$ satisfying $f\left(1\right) + f\left(2\right) = f\left(4\right) - 1$ is equal to........
35176.sol:
Given,

$f ( 1 ) + f\left(2\right) + 1 = f\left(4\right)$

$⇒ f\left(1\right) + f\left(2\right) \le 5$ $\left\{\text{as}f\left(4\right) \le 6\right\}$

Now taking cases we get,

Case $\left(1\right), f\left(1\right) = 1 ⇒ f\left(2\right) = \left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\} \to 4\text{mappings}$

Case $\left(2\right), f\left(1\right) = 2 ⇒ f\left(2\right) = \left\{1, 2, 3\right\} \to 3\text{mappings}$

Case $\left(3\right), f\left(1\right) = 3 ⇒ f\left(2\right) = \left\{1, 2\right\} \to 2\text{mappings}$

Case $\left(4\right), f\left(1\right) = 4 ⇒ f\left(2\right) = \left\{1\right\} \to 1\text{mappings}$

And $f\left(5\right) \text{ and } f\left(6\right) \to 6\text{mapping each}$

So, total number of function will be $= \left(4 + 3 + 2 + 1\right) \times 6 \times 6 = 360$

35728.text: If $\lim_{n \to \infty}\left(\sqrt{{n}^{2} - n - 1} + n\alpha + \beta\right) = 0$ then $8\left(\alpha + \beta\right)$ is equal to
35728.sol:
Given, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\sqrt{{n}^{2} - n - 1} + \alphan + \beta = 0$

Now rewriting the expression we get,

$\lim_{n \to \infty}\left({n}^{2} - n - 1\right)\dfrac{1}{2} + \alphan = - \beta$

$⇒\lim_{n \to \infty}n\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n} - \dfrac{1}{{n}^{2}}\right)\dfrac{1}{2} + \alphan = - \beta$

Now on using binomial approximation ${\left(1 + x\right)}^{n} = 1 + nx$ we get,

$\lim_{n \to \infty}n\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2n} - \dfrac{1}{2{n}^{2}}\right) + \alphan = - \beta$

$⇒ \lim_{n \to \infty}n - \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2n} + \alphan = - \beta$

$⇒ \lim_{n \to \infty}n\left(1 + \alpha\right) - \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2n} = - \beta$

Now for limit to exist $\left(1 + \alpha\right) = 0 ⇒ \alpha = - 1$

Now on putting the value of $\alpha$ we get,

$\lim_{n \to \infty}n\left(1 + \alpha\right) - \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2n} = - \beta$

$⇒ \lim_{n \to \infty} - \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2n} = - \beta$

$⇒ - \dfrac{1}{2} - 0 = - \beta$

$⇒ \beta = \dfrac{1}{2}$

So, $8\left(\alpha + \beta\right) = 8\left(- 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 8 \times \dfrac{- 1}{2} = - 4$

37127.text: Let ${a}_{n}$ be ${n}^{th}$ term of the series $5 + 8 + 14 + 23 + 35 + 50 + . . . . . . .$and ${S}_{n} = \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{n}{a}_{k}$. Then ${S}_{30} - {a}_{40}$ is equal to
37127.sol:
The given series is ${a}_{n}$, then we can write as

${a}_{n} = 5 + 8 + 14 + 23 + . . . . . . . . . . . . + {a}_{n}{a}_{n} = 5 + 8 + 14 + 23 + . . . . . . + {a}_{n - 1} + {a}_{n}$

Subtracting above equations, we get

$0 = 5 + 3 + 6 + 9 + . . . . + \left({a}_{n} - {a}_{n - 1}\right) - {a}_{n}$

$⇒ {a}_{n} = 5 + \left[\dfrac{\left(n - 1\right)}{2}\left(2 \times 3 + \left(n - 1 - 1\right)3\right)\right]$

$⇒ {a}_{n} = 5 + \dfrac{\left(n - 1\right)}{2}\left(3n\right)$

$⇒ {a}_{n} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3{n}^{2} - 3n + 10\right)$

So,

$⇒ {a}_{40} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3 \times {40}^{2} - 3 \times 40 + 10\right)$

$⇒ {a}_{40} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(4800 - 120 + 10\right)$

$⇒ {a}_{40} = 2345$

$⇒ {S}_{30} = \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{30}{a}_{n}$

$⇒ {S}_{30} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(3\mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{30}\left({n}^{2}\right) - 3\mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{30}\left(n\right) + \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{30}10\right)$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3\left(30\right)\left(31\right)\left(61\right)}{6} - \dfrac{3\left(30\right)\left(31\right)}{2} + 10 \times 30\right)$

$⇒ {S}_{30} = 13635$

$⇒ {S}_{30} - {a}_{40} = 13635 - 2345 = 11290$

Therefore, the required value is $11290$.

37739.text: Let ${m}_{1}, {m}_{2}$ be the slopes of two adjacent sides of a square of side $a$ such that ${a}^{2} + 11a + 3\left({m}_{1}^{2} + {m}_{2}^{2}\right) = 220$. 37739.sol:

Also given ${a}^{2} + 11a + 3\left({m}_{1}^{2} + {m}_{2}^{2}\right) = 220$

$⇒ {a}^{2} + 11a + 3\left({m}_{1}^{2} + 1{m}_{1}^{2}\right) = 220$

Now on plotting the diagram we get,

Now given equation of $AC$,

$\left(cos\alpha - sin\alpha\right)x + \left(sin\alpha + cos\alpha\right)y = 10$

Now by property of square we know that diagonals are perpendicular to each other

So equation of $BD$ will be $\left(sin\alpha + cos\alpha\right)x + \left(sin\alpha - cos\alpha\right)y + \lambda = 0$ now is passes through $D\left(10\left(cos\alpha - sin\alpha\right), 10\left(sin\alpha - cos\alpha\right)\right)$,

So, equation of $BD = \left(sin\alpha + cos\alpha\right)x + \left(sin\alpha - cos\alpha\right)y = 0$

Now slope of $AB \text{ and } AD$ will be given by angle bisector equation of $AC \text{ and } BD$

$\dfrac{\left(cos\alpha - sin\alpha\right)x + \left(sin\alpha + cos\alpha\right)y - 10}{\sqrt{2}} = \pm \dfrac{\left(sin\alpha + cos\alpha\right)x + \left(sin\alpha - cos\alpha\right)y}{\sqrt{2}}$

Taking positive sign we get,

$- 2sin\alphax + 2cos\alphay - 10 = 0$, so slope ${m}_{1} = tan\alpha$

Now taking negative sign we get,

$2cos\alphax + 2sin\alphay - 10 = 0$, so slope ${m}_{2} = - \text{cot}\alpha$

Now finding $a$ by using distance of point from line

Now we can see distance of $D$ from $AC$ will be $\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$,

So, $\dfrac{10{\left(cos\alpha - sin\alpha\right)}^{2} + 10{\left(cos\alpha - sin\alpha\right)}^{2} - 10}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ a = 10$

Now putting the value of $a, {m}_{1} \text{ and } {m}_{2} in {a}^{2} + 11a + 3\left({m}_{1}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{m}_{1}2}\right) = 220$ we get,

$⇒ 100 + 110 + 3\left(\tan^{2}\alpha + {cot}^{2}\alpha\right) = 220$

$⇒ 210 + 3\left(\tan^{2}\alpha + {cot}^{2}\alpha\right) = 220$

$⇒ 3\left(\tan^{2}\alpha + {cot}^{2}\alpha\right) = 10$

$⇒ \left(\tan^{2}\alpha + {cot}^{2}\alpha\right) = \dfrac{10}{3}$

So this is only possible when $\tan^{2}\alpha = 3 \text{$ and $} {\text{cot}}^{2}\alpha = \dfrac{1}{3}$ or vice versa

So, $72\left(\sin^{4}\alpha + \cos^{4}\alpha\right) + {a}^{2} - 3a + 13$

$= 72\left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right) + 83 = 45 + 83 = 128$

38284.text: A line with direction cosines proportional to $2,1,2$ meets each of the lines $x=y+a=z$ and $x+a=2 y=2 z$. The co-ordinates of each of the point of intersection are given by
38284.sol:
Any point on the line $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+a}{1}=\frac{z}{1}=t_1 \quad$ (say) is $\left(t_1, t_1-a, t_1\right)$ and any point on the line $\frac{x+a}{2}=\frac{y}{1}=\frac{z}{1}=t_2 \quad($ say $)$ is $\left(2 t_2-a, t_2, t_2\right)$.
Now direction cosine of the lines intersecting the above lines is proportional to $\left(2 t_2-a-t_1, t_2-t_1+a, t_2-t_1\right)$.
Hence $2 \mathrm{t}_2-\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{t}_1=2 \mathrm{k}, \mathrm{t}_2-\mathrm{t}_1+\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{k}$ and $\mathrm{t}_2-\mathrm{t}_1=2 \mathrm{k}$
On solving these, we get $t_1=3 a, t_2=a$.
Hence points are $(3 a, 2 a, 3 a) and (a, a, a)$

39525.text: In a meter bridge experiment to determine the value of unknown resistance, first the resistances $2 \Omega$ and $3 \Omega$ are connected in the left and right gaps of the bridge and the null point is obtained at a distance $l \mathrm{~cm}$ from the left. Now when an unknown resistance $x \Omega$ is connected in parallel to $3 \Omega$ resistance, the null point is shifted by 10 cm to the right of wire. The value of unknown resistance $x$ is $\_\_\_\_$ $\Omega$.
39525.sol:
Meter bridge null point condition: $\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{l}{100-l}$
Initial: $R_1 = 2Ω$, $R_2 = 3Ω$, null at $l$ cm
$\frac{2}{3} = \frac{l}{100-l}$ gives $2(100-l) = 3l$, so $l = 40$ cm
When $xΩ$ connected in parallel with $3Ω$: $R_2' = \frac{3x}{3+x}Ω$
New null point at $(40+10) = 50$ cm from left:
$\frac{2}{R_2'} = \frac{50}{50} = 1$
$\frac{2(3+x)}{3x} = 1$ gives $6 + 2x = 3x$
$x = 6Ω$

40076.text: The de-Broglie wavelength $\left({\lambda}_{B}\right)$ associated with the electron orbiting in the second excited state of hydrogen atom is related to that in the ground state $\left({\lambda}_{G}\right)$ by:
40076.sol:
We know that wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum, let ${\lambda}_{B}$ is de-Broglie Wavelength corresponds to momentum ${P}_{B}$, similarly let ${\lambda}_{G}$ is Wavelength at ground state corresponds to momentum${P}_{G}$,
$\dfrac{{\lambda}_{B}}{{\lambda}_{G}} = \dfrac{{P}_{G}}{{P}_{B}} = \dfrac{m{v}_{G}}{m{v}_{B}}$, and velocity, $V ∝ \dfrac{z}{n}$, where $Z$ is the atomic number, and $n$ is a number of orbits, here, ${n}_{G} = 1$ (ground state), ${n}_{B} = 3$ (second excited state). So, $\dfrac{{\lambda}_{B}}{{\lambda}_{G}} = \dfrac{{n}_{B}}{{n}_{G}} = \dfrac{3}{1}$$⇒ {\lambda}_{B} = 3{\lambda}_{G}$

$⇒ s = 18m$

50101.subject: Physics
50101.text:
An electron falls through a distance $1.5$ cm in $2.0 \times 10^4$ N/C from rest. The time taken to cover this distance in second is ____
$(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}, m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg})$
50101.sol:
Force on the electron is $F = eE$

Acceleration of the electron is $a = \dfrac{eE}{m_e}$

Using the equation of motion $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

Since the electron starts from rest, $u = 0$

$s = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{eE}{m_e} \right) t^2$

$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2sm_e}{eE}}$

Substituting the given values:

$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.0 \times 10^4}}$

$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{27.33 \times 10^{-33}}{3.2 \times 10^{-15}}}$

$t = \sqrt{8.54 \times 10^{-18}}$

$t \approx 2.9 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s}$

Answer: $2.9 \times 10^{-9}$

54665.text: A circular disc is rotating with angular velocity $\omega$. If a man standing at the edge of the disc walks towards its centre then the angular velocity of the disc will
54665.sol:
When no external force acts on a body its angular moment remains conserved.
From law of conservation of angular momentum, we have
$J=l \omega=$ constant
where $/$ is moment of inertia of the body and $\omega$ is angular velocity.
Also $I=\frac{1}{2} M R^2$ (for disc) where $M$ is mass and $R$ is radius of disc.
$J=\frac{1}{2} M R^2 \omega=$ constant
Since, man moves towards the centre of the disc, distance of mass distribution $R$ decreases hence, $\omega$ increases.

54896.subject: Chemistry
54896.text: Which among the following has lowest boiling point?
54896.sol:
Boiling point comparisons for aldehydes rely primarily on molecular weight and intermolecular forces.
Increasing molecular weight enhances van der Waals interactions, raising boiling points.

Molecular weights correspond to carbon counts:

56059.text: Half life of a first order reaction $is 900 minute at 400 K , find its half life at 300 K ? \left(\frac{\mathrm{Ea}}{2 \cdot 303 \mathrm{R}}=$1 \cdot 3056 \times 10^3\right)
56059.sol:
For a first-order reaction, the half-life relates to the rate constant by $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$.

The Arrhenius equation connects rate constants at two temperatures as $\log \left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = \frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right).

Given $ t_{1/2,1} = 900$ minutes at $T_1 = 400$ K, and \frac{E_a}{2.303R} =1.3056 \times10^3$ K, the half-life at $T_2 = 300$ K can be found by relating the ratios. Since $\frac{t_{1/2,2}}{t_{1/2,1}} =\frac{k_1}{k_2}$,

$\log $\$left(\frac{t_{1/2,2}}{900}\right) = \frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{T_1 - T_2}{T_1 T_2}\right).

Substituting the values:

$$\log\$$left(\frac{t_{1/2,2}}{900}\right) = ($1.3056 \times 10^3) \$left(\frac{400 - 300}{400 \times 300}\right) = ($1.3056 \times 10^3) \$left(\frac{1}{1200}\right) \approx$1.088$.

Thus, \frac{t_{1/2,2}}{900} =$10^{1.088} \approx 12.246$, so $t_{1/2,2} \approx 11021.4$ minutes.

The value corresponds to option B.

$

59150.subject: Chemistry
59150.text: Calculate van't Hoff factor of aqueous solution of 0.18 m electrolyte that freezes at $-0.54^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}  \left($$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}$$} \text{$ for solvent }=1.86 $\mathrm{ K} \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}$\right)
59150.sol:
The van't Hoff factor $i$ is determined using the freezing point depression formula:

$\Delta T_f = i \cdot K_f \cdot m$

Given molality $m = 0.18\, \text{m}$, solution freezing point $T_f = -0.54^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$, cryoscopic constant $K_f = 1.86\, \text{K}\,\text{kg}\,\text{mol}^{-1}$, and pure water freezing point $T_f^0 = 0^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$, the depression is:

$\Delta T_f = T_f^0 - T_f = 0 - (-0.54) = 0.54\, \text{K}$

Solving for $i$:

$i = \frac{\Delta T_f}{K_f \cdot m} = \frac{0.54}{1.86 \cdot 0.18} = \frac{0.54}{0.3348} \approx 1.6129$

This value approximates to $1.612$, corresponding to option C.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

62018.sol:
To determine $(f {}^{\circ} g)^{-1}(x)$, the composite function $(f {}^{\circ} g)(x)$ must first be found, then inverted.

Given $f(x) = 3x + 10$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 1$, the composition is:
$(f {}^{\circ} g)(x) = f(g(x)) = 3(x^2 - 1) + 10 = 3x^2 + 7$

Let $y = (f {}^{\circ} g)(x) = 3x^2 + 7$. Interchanging $x$ and $y$ and solving for $y$:
$x = 3y^2 + 7 \implies y^2 = \frac{x - 7}{3} \implies y = \pm\sqrt{\frac{x - 7}{3}}$

Since the options only include the principal root, we take:
$(f {}^{\circ} g)^{-1}(x) = \left(\frac{x - 7}{3}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$

This corresponds to option B.

62525.subject: Mathematics
62525.sol:
Given equation: $\sin(\cos^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}x) - \cos(\sin^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}x) = \sin(\cot^{-1}2)$

Let $\alpha = \cos^{-1}x$ and $\gamma = \tan^{-1}x$.

We know that $\sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $\sin^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \alpha$.

The second term on the left hand side becomes $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \alpha + \gamma\right) = \sin(\alpha - \gamma)$.

The left hand side simplifies to $\sin(\alpha + \gamma) - \sin(\alpha - \gamma) = 2 \cos\alpha \sin\gamma$.

Since $\alpha = \cos^{-1}x$, we have $\cos\alpha = x$.

Since $\gamma = \tan^{-1}x$, we have $\sin\gamma = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$.

Thus, the left hand side is $2x \left( \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} \right) = \dfrac{2x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$.

For the right hand side, let $\theta = \cot^{-1}2$, then $\cot\theta = 2$, which gives $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+\cot^2\theta}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$.

Equating both sides:

$\dfrac{2x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$

Squaring both sides:

$\dfrac{4x^4}{1+x^2} = \dfrac{1}{5}$

$20x^4 = 1 + x^2$

$20x^4 - x^2 - 1 = 0$

$(5x^2 + 1)(4x^2 - 1) = 0$

Since $x^2 > 0$, we must have $4x^2 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Given $x > 0$, we get $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$

62824.subject: Mathematics
62824.text: In L.P.P., the corner points of the feasible region for the constraints $3x - y \geq 6, x \leq 3, y \leq 2, y \geq 0, x \geq 0$ are.....
62824.sol:
The given constraints are $3x - y \geq 6$, $x \leq 3$, $y \leq 2$, $x \geq 0$, $y \geq 0$.

The boundary lines for the feasible region are $3x - y = 6$, $x = 3$, $y = 2$, $x = 0$, and $y = 0$.

Finding the intersection points of the line $3x - y = 6$ with the other boundary lines:
Intersection with $y = 0$: $3x - 0 = 6 \Rightarrow x = 2$. The point is $(2, 0)$.
Intersection with $y = 2$: $3x - 2 = 6 \Rightarrow 3x = 8 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{8}{3}$. The point is $\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 2\right)$.

The other corner points are formed by the intersection of the remaining boundary lines $x = 3$, $y = 2$, and $y = 0$ that satisfy $3x - y \geq 6$:
Intersection of $x = 3 and y = 0$ is $(3, 0)$.
Intersection of $x = 3 and y = 2$ is $(3, 2)$.

Checking these points against all constraints:
For $(2, 0)$: $3(2) - 0 = 6 \geq 6$, $2 \leq 3$, $0 \leq 2$. (Satisfies all)
For $\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 2\right)$: $3\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) - 2 = 6 \geq 6$, $\dfrac{8}{3} \leq 3$, $2 \leq 2$. (Satisfies all)
For $(3, 2)$: $3(3) - 2 = 7 \geq 6$, $3 \leq 3$, $2 \leq 2$. (Satisfies all)
For $(3, 0)$: $3(3) - 0 = 9 \geq 6$, $3 \leq 3$, $0 \leq 2$. (Satisfies all)

Thus, the corner points of the feasible region are $\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 2\right), (3, 2), (3, 0), (2, 0)$.

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 2\right), (3, 2), (3, 0), (2, 0)$

64403.text: If the centroid of a tetrahedron $OABC$ is $(1, 2, -1)$, where O is the origin, $A(a, 2, 3), B(1, b, 2), C(2, 1, c)$ are the other vertices, then the distance of the point $P(a, b, c)$ from the origin is...
64403.sol:
The coordinates of the centroid of a tetrahedron with vertices $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$, $(x_2, y_2, z_2)$, $(x_3, y_3, z_3)$, and $(x_4, y_4, z_4)$ are given by $\left( \dfrac{x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4}{4}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2 + y_3 + y_4}{4}, \dfrac{z_1 + z_2 + z_3 + z_4}{4} \right)$.

Given the vertices $O(0, 0, 0)$, $A(a, 2, 3)$, $B(1, b, 2)$, and $C(2, 1, c)$, and the centroid $(1, 2, -1)$, equating the coordinates gives:

$\dfrac{0 + a + 1 + 2}{4} = 1 \Rightarrow a + 3 = 4 \Rightarrow a = 1$

$\dfrac{0 + 2 + b + 1}{4} = 2 \Rightarrow b + 3 = 8 \Rightarrow b = 5$

$\dfrac{0 + 3 + 2 + c}{4} = -1 \Rightarrow c + 5 = -4 \Rightarrow c = -9$

The point $P(a, b, c)$ is $(1, 5, -9)$.

The distance of $P$ from the origin is:

$OP = \sqrt{1^2 + 5^2 + (-9)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 25 + 81} = \sqrt{107}$ units.

Answer: $\sqrt{107}$ units

64413.sol:
The line passes through $P(-1, 2, 3)$ and is perpendicular to both $L_1$ and $L_2.$

The direction vector of $L_1$ is $\vec{d_1} = (2, -3, -2)$ and for $L_2$ it is $\vec{d_2} = (-1, 2, 3).$ Since the required line is perpendicular to both, its direction vector is the cross product $\vec{d} = \vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2}.$

$\vec{d} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} \text{ and } \mathbf{j} \text{ and } \mathbf{k} \\ 2 \text{ and } -3 \text{ and } -2 \\ -1 \text{ and } 2 \text{ and } 3 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}((-3)(3) - (-2)(2)) - \mathbf{j}((2)(3) - (-2)(-1)) + \mathbf{k}((2)(2) - (-3)(-1))$

Computing yields $\vec{d} = -5\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} + 1\mathbf{k} = (-5, -4, 1).$

A line through $(-1, 2, 3)$ with direction $(-5, -4, 1)$ has symmetric form $\frac{x + 1}{-5} = \frac{y - 2}{-4} = \frac{z - 3}{1}.$ Multiplying denominators by $-1$ gives the equivalent form $\frac{x + 1}{5} = \frac{y - 2}{4} = \frac{z - 3}{-1}.$

The correct answer is option C.

64430.text: If the plane $\frac{x}{2}+\frac{y}{3}+\frac{z}{6}=1$ cuts the co - ordinate axes at points $A, B, C$ respectively, then area of the triangle ABC is
64430.sol:
The plane given by $\frac{x}{2} + \frac{y}{3} + \frac{z}{6} = 1$ intercepts the coordinate axes at $A = (2, 0, 0)$, $B = (0, 3, 0)$, and $C = (0, 0, 6)$, forming triangle $ABC$.

Vectors representing two sides are $\vec{AB} = (-2, 3, 0)$ and $\vec{AC} = (-2, 0, 6)$.
The cross product yields $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = (18, 12, 6)$ with magnitude $|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}| = \sqrt{18^2 + 12^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{504} = 6\sqrt{14}$.

The area of triangle $ABC$ is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 6\sqrt{14} = 3\sqrt{14}$ square units.
Alternatively, using the intercept formula $\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{(ab)^2 + (bc)^2 + (ca)^2}$ with $a=2$, $b=3$, $c=6$ gives the same result:

$\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{(6)^2 + (18)^2 + (12)^2} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{504} = 3\sqrt{14}$.

Final answer: $3\sqrt{14}$ square units

66663.subject: Physics
66663.text: When an electron in a hydrogen atom jumps from the third excited state to the ground state, the de-Broglie wavelength associated with the electron becomes
66663.sol:
The De Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{h}{p}$, where $h=$ Planck's constant and $p=$ momentum of the electron. Also, momentum $p=m v$ and kinetic energy $E_K=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$ From the above equation, we can relate momentum $p$ and kinetic energy $E_K$ as, $p=\sqrt{2 m E_K}$
Now the ratio of wavelength of hydrogen atom when the atom jumps from third excited state to ground state viz $(n=4$ to $n=1$ )
$\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{\frac{h}{p_1}}{\frac{h}{p_2}}=\frac{p_2}{p_1}=\sqrt{\frac{E_{K 2}}{E_{K 1}}}-\cdots(1)$
Also, we know $E_{K n}=\frac{-13.6 Z^2}{n^2}$
Using equation (1),
$\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{\sqrt{1^2}}{\sqrt{4^2}}$
So, the ratio of the wavelength of ground state $\{n=1\}$ to $3^{\text{rd }}$ excited state $\{n=4\}$ is $\frac{1}{4}$.

66815.subject: Physics
66815.text: A coil of self-inductance $L$ is connected in series with a bulb and an a.c. source. Brightness of the bulb decreases when
options: an iron rod is inserted in the coil.
frequency of a.c. source is decreased.
number of turns in the coil is reduced.
$a capacitance of reactance  \left(X_C-X_L\right) is included in the same circuit.$
66815.sol:
The brightness of the bulb depends on the power dissipated, given by $P = I^2 R$, so it decreases when the RMS current $I$ decreases.

In an AC series circuit with the bulb (resistance $R$) and coil (inductive reactance $X_L$), the impedance is $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}$ and the current is $I = V/Z$. A decrease in current requires an increase in impedance, which occurs when $X_L$ increases since $X_L = 2\pi f L$.

Inserting an iron rod into the coil increases the magnetic permeability, raising the inductance $L$. This increases $X_L$, thus increasing $Z$ and decreasing $I$, which reduces brightness.

Decreasing the AC source frequency reduces $X_L$, decreasing $Z$ and increasing both $I$ and brightness.

Reducing the number of turns in the coil decreases $L$ (since $L \propto N^2$), reducing $X_L$ and $Z$, and increasing brightness.

Including a capacitance with specified reactance leads to impedance $Z' = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, which may increase or decrease depending on $X_C$. Since brightness reduction is not guaranteed, this option is incorrect.

The correct choice is $\boxed{A}$.

67016.text: If two charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ are separated with distance 'd' and placed in a medium of dielectric constant $K$. What will be the equivalent distance between charges in air for the same electrostatic force?
67016.sol:
Force between charges in a medium of dielectric constant $K$ is given by $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0 K} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{d^2}$.

Force between charges in air at an equivalent distance $d'$ is given by $F' = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{d'^2}$.

For the same electrostatic force, $F = F'$.

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0 K} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{d^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{d'^2}$

$\dfrac{1}{K d^2} = \dfrac{1}{d'^2}$

$d'^2 = K d^2$

$d' = d \sqrt{K} = d[K]^{1/2}$

Answer: $d[k]^{1/2}$

67685.subject: Physics
67685.text: In hydrogen atom, an electron of charge ' e ' revolves in an orbit of radius ' $r$ ' with speed ' $v$ '. The magnetic moment associated with electron is
67685.sol:
The magnetic moment of a current loop is given by $\mu = IA$, where $I$ is the current and $A$ is the area enclosed. For an electron with charge $e$ revolving in a circular orbit of radius $r$ with speed $v$, the current is $I = \frac{e}{T} = \frac{e}{2\pi r/v} = \frac{ev}{2\pi r}$. The area is $A = \pi r^2$.

Substituting these expressions yields $\mu = \left(\frac{ev}{2\pi r}\right) \left(\pi r^2\right) = \frac{evr}{2}$.

The magnetic moment is therefore $\frac{evr}{2}$, corresponding to option B.

67699.text: Two identical long parallel wires carry currents ' $\mathrm{I}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{I}_2$ ' such that $\mathrm{I}_1 > \mathrm{I}_2$. When the currents are in the same direction, the magnetic field at a point midway between the wires is $8 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{ T}$. If the direction of $\mathrm{I}_2$ is reversed, the field becomes $3.2 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ T}$. The ratio of $\mathrm{I}_2$ to $\mathrm{I}_1$ is
67699.sol:
The distance from the midway point between two parallel wires to either wire is $r = \frac{d}{2}$. The magnetic field at this point due to each wire is $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, giving $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{\pi d}$ and $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I_2}{\pi d}$.

When currents flow in the same direction, the magnetic fields oppose. With $I_1 > I_2$, the net field is $B_{\text{net1}} = \frac{\mu_0}{\pi d}(I_1 - I_2) = 8 \times 10^{-6}\, \text{T}$.

Reversing $I_2$ makes the fields additive: $B_{\text{net2}} = \frac{\mu_0}{\pi d}(I_1 + I_2) = 3.2 \times 10^{-5}\, \text{T}$.

Dividing these equations gives $\frac{I_1 + I_2}{I_1 - I_2} = 4$.

Solving yields $I_1 + I_2 = 4(I_1 - I_2)$, which simplifies to $5I_2 = 3I_1$.

The ratio is $\frac{I_2}{I_1} = \frac{3}{5}$.

Answer: C

68163.text: A capillary tube is taken from earth's surface to moon's surface. The rise of liquid column on the moon's surface is (acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface is six times that of moon's surface)
options: six times that on the earth's surface.
equal to that on the earth's surface.
68163.sol:
The height of the liquid column is determined by the equation $h = \frac{2T \cos\theta}{\rho g r}$, where $g$ is the only variable when moving from Earth to the Moon.

Given that $g_E = 6g_M$, we substitute $g_M = \frac{g_E}{6}$ into the height expression for the Moon:

$h_M = \frac{2T \cos\theta}{\rho (g_E/6) r} = 6 \cdot \frac{2T \cos\theta}{\rho g_E r} = 6h_E$.

Therefore, the rise on the Moon is six times that on Earth, and the correct answer is B.

69720.subject: Physics
69720.text: Rate of flow of heat through a cylindrical rod is '$H_1$'. The temperature at the ends of the rod are $T_1$ and $T_2$. If all the dimensions of the rod become double and the temperature difference remains the same and if the rate of flow of heat becomes '$H_2$' then $H_2 =$
69720.sol:
The rate of flow of heat through a rod is given by $H = \dfrac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

For a cylindrical rod of radius $r$ and length $L$, the area of cross-section is $A = \pi r^2$.

Initial rate of heat flow is $H_1 = \dfrac{K \pi r^2 (T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

When all dimensions are doubled, the new radius is $r' = 2r$ and the new length is $L' = 2L$.

The new rate of heat flow is $H_2 = \dfrac{K \pi (2r)^2 (T_1 - T_2)}{2L}$

$H_2 = \dfrac{4 K \pi r^2 (T_1 - T_2)}{2L}$

$H_2 = 2 \left( \dfrac{K \pi r^2 (T_1 - T_2)}{L} \right)

$H_2 = 2H_1$

Answer: 2\text{H}_1$

70034.text: A gas is compressed at a constant pressure of $50 \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2$ from a volume of $10 \mathrm{ m}^3$ to a volume of $4 \mathrm{ m}^3$. Energy of $100 \mathrm{ J}$ is then added to the gas by heating. Its internal energy is

$\mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\Delta \mathrm{W}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\mathrm{P} \Delta \mathrm{V}$
Change in yolume due to compression

Negatiye sign indicates gas is compressed.
$\therefore \quad \Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{P} \Delta \mathrm{V}=100-[50 \times(-6)]=400 \mathrm{ J}$
As, $\Delta \mathrm{U}$ is positive, the internal energy is increased.

70414.text: The third overtone of a closed pipe of length '$L_c$' has the same frequency as the third overtone of the open pipe of length '$L_0$'. Both the pipes have same diameters. The ratio $L_c : L_0$ is equal to
70414.sol:
For a closed pipe, the frequency of the $n$-th overtone is given by $f_c = (2n + 1) \dfrac{v}{4L_c}$.

For the third overtone ($n = 3$), the frequency is $f_c = 7 \dfrac{v}{4L_c}$.

For an open pipe, the frequency of the $n$-th overtone is given by $f_o = (n + 1) \dfrac{v}{2L_0}$.

For the third overtone ($n = 3$), the frequency is $f_o = 4 \dfrac{v}{2L_0} = \dfrac{2v}{L_0}$.

Given that the frequencies of the third overtones are equal:

$7 \dfrac{v}{4L_c} = \dfrac{2v}{L_0}$

$\dfrac{L_c}{L_0} = \dfrac{7}{8}$

The ratio $L_c : L_0$ is $7:8$.

Answer: $7:8$

70934.subject: Biology
70934.text: Which one of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding genetic diversity?
options: Allelic genes lead to individual differences within species.
Existence of subspecies, races are examples of genetic diversity.
It includes variation within a population
70934.sol:
Genetic diversity refers to the variation of genes within a single species, which is known as intraspecific diversity. Interspecific diversity refers to the diversity between different species, which is termed species diversity.

Allelic variations lead to individual differences within a species, and the existence of subspecies or races are examples of genetic diversity. It also includes variations within a population.

Therefore, the statement that genetic diversity is interspecific diversity is incorrect.

Answer: Genetic diversity is interspecific diversity

71886.subject: Chemistry
71886.text: The solubility product of aluminium hydroxide at $298$ K is $4.2 \times 10^{-14}$. Calculate its solubility in mol/L at same temperature.
71886.sol:
The dissociation of aluminium hydroxide is given by:

$Al(OH)_3 \rightleftharpoons Al^{3+} + 3OH^-$

Let the solubility of $Al(OH)_3$ be $s$ mol/L.

$[Al^{3+}] = s$

$[OH^-] = 3s$

The solubility product $K_{sp}$ is given by:

$K_{sp} = [Al^{3+}][OH^-]^3$

$K_{sp} = (s)(3s)^3 = 27s^4$

Given $K_{sp} = 4.2 \times 10^{-14}$:

$27s^4 = 4.2 \times 10^{-14}$

$s^4 = \dfrac{4.2 \times 10^{-14}}{27} = 15.55 \times 10^{-16}$

$s = (15.55)^{1/4} \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.987 \times 10^{-4}$ mol/L

Answer: $1.987 \times 10^{-4}$

72202.subject: Physics
72202.text: The electric potential 'V' as a function of distance x (in metre) is $V = 4x^2 + 6x - 8$ volt. Electric field at $x = 2$ m is
72202.sol:
The relation between electric field $E$ and electric potential $V$ is given by $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}$.

Given $V = 4x^2 + 6x - 8$.

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{dV}{dx} = \dfrac{d}{dx}(4x^2 + 6x - 8) = 8x + 6$

Therefore, $E = -(8x + 6)$.

At $x = 2$ m:

$E = -(8(2) + 6) = -(16 + 6) = -22\ \text{V/m}$.

Answer: $-22\ \text{V/m}$

If
$\begin{aligned}
& \cos A+\cos B=m \\
& \sin A+\sin B=n
\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}
& m n=\sin \mathrm{A} \cdot \cos \mathrm{ A}+\sin \mathrm{A} \cdot \cos \mathrm{ B} \\
& \quad+\quad \cos \mathrm{A} \cdot \sin \mathrm{ B}+\cos \mathrm{B} \cdot \sin \mathrm{ B} \\
& =\frac{\sin 2 \mathrm{ A}}{2}+\sin (\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B})+\frac{\sin 2 \mathrm{ B}}{2} \\
& =\sin (\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B})+\frac{1}{2}\{2 \sin (\mathrm{ A}+\mathrm{B}) \cdot \cos (\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{B})\} \\
& =\sin (\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B})+\sin (\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}) \cdot \cos (\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{B}) \\
& m n=\sin (\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B})\{1+\cos (\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{B})\}...(i)
\end{aligned}$

\end{aligned}$

89465.text:
A balloon has a volume 400 ml at $0 ° C$. The balloon is distended to 4/5th of its maximum stretching capacity.
(i) Will burst if it is brought into a room at $40 ° C$ ?
(ii) What is the maximum temperature above which it will burst?
options: Balloon will not burst at $40 °$ C, balloon will burst above 40 $°$ C
Balloon will burst at $40 °$ C, balloon will not burst above 68.25 $°$ C
Balloon will not burst at $40 °$ C, balloon will burst above 68.25 $°$ C
89465.sol:
(i) Maximum stretching capacity $= 400 \times \dfrac{5}{4} = 500$ ml
$\dfrac{{V}_{1}}{{T}_{1}} = \dfrac{{V}_{2}}{{T}_{2}}$
or $\dfrac{400}{273} = \dfrac{{V}_{2}}{313}$
${V}_{2} = 458.61$ ml
If the volume becomes more than 500 ml it will burst. The volume is below 500 ml, hence it will not burst at 40 $° C$ .
(ii) $\dfrac{{V}_{1}}{{T}_{1}} = \dfrac{{V}_{2}}{{T}_{2}}$
or $\dfrac{400}{273} = \dfrac{500}{{T}_{2}}$
${T}_{2} = 341.25$ K = 68.25 $° C$
The temperature at which the volume becomes 500 ml the balloon will burst. So balloon burst above 68.26 $° C$.

93990.text: Two radioactive nuclei $P$ and $Q$, in a given sample decay into a stable nucleus $R$. At time $t = 0$, the number of $P$ species are $4{N}_{0}$ and that of $Q$ is ${N}_{0}$. The half-life of $P$ (for conversion to $R$) is $1minute$ whereas that of $Q$ is $2minutes$. Initially, there are no nuclei of $R$ present in the sample. When the number of nuclei of $P$ and $Q$ is equal, the number of nuclei of $R$ present in the sample would be
93990.sol:
$\begin{array}{ll}\text{P} & \text{Q} \\ \text{No. of nuclei, at t = 0} & 4{N}_{0} & {N}_{0} \\ \text{Half-life} & \text{1 min} & \text{2 min} \\ \text{No. of nuclei after} & {N}_{P} & {N}_{Q} \\ \text{time t}\end{array}$

Let after t min, the number of nuclei of $P$ and $Q$ are equal.

$∴ {N}_{P} = 4{N}_{0}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)t / 1\text{and}{N}_{Q} = {N}_{0}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)t / 2$

As ${N}_{P} = {N}_{Q}$

$∴ 4{N}_{0}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)t / 1 = {N}_{0}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)t / 2$

$\dfrac{4}{2t / 1} = \dfrac{1}{2t / 2}\text{or}4 = \dfrac{2t}{2t / 2}$

or $4 = {2}^{t / 2}or{2}^{2} = {2}^{t / 2}$

$\text{or}\dfrac{t}{2} = 2\text{or}\text{t} = 4min$

After $4minutes$, both $P$ and $Q$ have an equal number of nuclei.

∴ Number of nuclei of $R$

$= \left(4{N}_{0} - \dfrac{N0}{4}\right) +\left({N}_{0} - \dfrac{N0}{4}\right)

$= $\dfrac{15{N}_{0}}{4} + \dfrac{3{N}_{0}}{4} = \dfrac{9{N}_{0}}{2}$

94847.text: The period of oscillation of a simple pendulum is given by $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$, where $L$ is the length of the pendulum and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. The length is measured using a meter scale which has $500$ divisions. If the measured value $L$ is $50$ cm, the accuracy in the determination of $g$ is $1.1%$ and the time taken for $100$ oscillations is $100$ seconds, what should be the possible error in measurement of the clock in one minute (in milliseconds)?

Given,

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$

or $T^{2} = 4{\pi}^{2}\dfrac{l}{g}$

$∴ 2\dfrac{∆ T}{T} = \dfrac{∆ l}{l} + \dfrac{∆ g}{g}$ ...(i)

Now, $l = 50cm, ∆ l = 2mm = 0.2cm$

$\dfrac{∆ g}{g} = 1.1% = \dfrac{1.1}{100}$

Put these values in Equation. (i), then we get

$\dfrac{∆ T}{T} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left[\dfrac{0.2}{50} + \dfrac{1.1}{100}\right]

$= 7.5 $\times {10}^{- 3}$ s$ or 7.5$ ms

$∵$ In $100$ s, resolution of the clock is $7 .5 ms$ .

$∴$ In $60$ s resolution of the clock is $\dfrac{7 .5 \times 60}{100}$ \approx$5$ ms

96611.subject: Botany
96611.text: Select the INCORRECT match from the following.
options: Primary productivity = amount of organic matter produced per unit area by photosynthesis
Productivity = The rate of biomass production
Gross primary productivity = rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers
96611.sol:
Gross primary production (GPP) is the rate at which an ecosystem's producers capture and store a given amount of chemical energy as biomass in a given length of time. (Definition). It is also the rate of conversion of light energy to chemical energy by producers in an ecosystem.

Total production of organic matter is called gross primary productivity and the energy left after utilization of producers is termed net primary productivity.

The rate of assimilation of food energy by consumers is called secondary productivity and this energy is available to carnivores as they are the consumers.

Net Primary Productivity (NPP) is the rate at which plants incorporate atmospheric carbon through photosynthesis. (Definition)

96668.subject: Botany
96668.text: Which of the following can accelerate the rate of decomposition of the detritus?
options: If the detritus contains lignin, chitin, tannins and cellulose
If the detritus is present in acidic soil
If the moisture and aeration are at optimum
If the temperature is below $10 ° C$
96668.sol:
Factors Affecting Decomposition: The rate of decomposition of detritus is controlled by the chemical nature of detritus and a number of climatic factors given below.
a) Chemical nature of detritus. Decomposition of detritus is slow if it contains lignin, chitin, tannins (phenolics) and cellulose. It is rapid if detritus possesses more of nitrogenous compounds (like proteins, nucleic acids) and water-soluble reserve carbohydrates or sugars.
b)Temperature and c) soil moisture is& the most important climatic factors that regulate decomposition through their effects on the activities of soil microbes.
d) Aeration: It is required for the activity of decomposers and detritivores. Reduced aeration will slow down the process of decomposition.

e) Salinity: The alkaline soil increase the detritus breakdown.
So, the warm and moist environment favour decomposition whereas low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition resulting in buildup of organic materials.

98152.subject: Chemistry
98152.text: Which of the following statement is correct about competitive inhibitors?
options: The inhibitor does not resembles the substrate.
The inhibitor competes with the substrate for the allosteric sites.
Inhibition of succinic hydrogenase by malonate which doesn't resemble the substrate succinate in structure is an example of it.
This mechanism is used in the control of bacterial pathogens.
98152.sol: When the inhibitor closely resembles the substrate in its molecular structure and inhibits the activity of the enzyme, it is known as a competitive inhibitor. Due to its close structural similarity with the substrate, the inhibitor competes with the substrate for the substrate-binding site of the enzyme. Consequently, the substrate cannot bind and as a result, the enzyme action declines, e.g., inhibition of succinic dehydrogenase by malonate which closely resembles the substrate succinate in structure. Such competitive inhibitors are often used in the control of bacterial pathogens.

102642.text:
A transverse harmonic wave on a string is described by $y(x, t) = 5 \sin\left( 4\pi t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} x \right)$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres and $t$ is in seconds. Match the wave parameters in List-I with their corresponding values in List-II.

List-IList-II
A. Amplitude (in m)I. $2$
B. Wavelength (in m)II. $5$
C. Frequency (in Hz)III. $6$
D. Wave velocity (in m/s)IV. $12$
102642.sol:
The given wave equation is $y = 5 \sin\left( 4\pi t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} x \right)$.
Comparing this with the standard equation $y = A \sin(\omega t - kx)$, we get:
Amplitude, $A = 5$ m (Matches with II)
Angular frequency, $\omega = 4\pi$ rad/s $\Rightarrow$ Frequency, $f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = 2$ Hz (Matches with I)
Angular wave number, $k = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ m$^{-1}$ $\Rightarrow$ Wavelength, $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = 6$ m (Matches with III)
Wave velocity, $v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{4\pi}{\pi/3} = 12$ m/s (Matches with IV)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

Answer: A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV

f_1=\frac{R}{(n-1)}\ldots(ii)
\end{gathered}$
Comparing Eqs. (i) and (ii), we see that focal length becomes double.
As power of lens $P \propto \frac{1}{\text{ focal length }}$ Hence, power will become half.
$\text{ New power }=\frac{4}{2}=2 $$\mathrm{D}$

107770.subject: Chemistry
107770.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Species)List-II (Properties)
(A) $\text{N}_2^+$(i) Bond order = $1$, Paramagnetic
(B) $\text{O}_2^-$(ii) Bond order = $2$, Diamagnetic
(C) $\text{C}_2$(iii) Bond order = $2.5$, Paramagnetic
(D) $\text{B}_2$(iv) Bond order = $1.5$, Paramagnetic

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
107770.sol:
The electronic configuration and properties of the given species are deduced using Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT):

1. $\text{N}_2^+$ ($13$ electrons): $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^{*} 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^{*} 2s^2 \pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2 \sigma 2p_z^1$.
Bond order = $\dfrac{9 - 4}{2} = 2.5$. It has one unpaired electron, hence it is paramagnetic. (A) matches with (iii).

2. $\text{O}_2^-$ ($17$ electrons): $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^{*} 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^{*} 2s^2 \sigma 2p_z^2 \pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2 \pi^{*} 2p_x^2 = \pi^{*} 2p_y^1$.
Bond order = $\dfrac{10 - 7}{2} = 1.5$. It has one unpaired electron, hence it is paramagnetic. (B) matches with (iv).

3. $\text{C}_2$ ($12$ electrons): $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^{*} 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^{*} 2s^2 \pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2$.
Bond order = $\dfrac{8 - 4}{2} = 2$. All electrons are paired, hence it is diamagnetic. (C) matches with (ii).

4. $\text{B}_2$ ($10$ electrons): $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^{*} 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^{*} 2s^2 \pi 2p_x^1 = \pi 2p_y^1$.
Bond order = $\dfrac{6 - 4}{2} = 1$. It has two unpaired electrons, hence it is paramagnetic. (D) matches with (i).

The correct matching is (A)-(iii), (B)-(iv), (C)-(ii), (D)-(i).

Answer: (A)-(iii), (B)-(iv), (C)-(ii), (D)-(i)

107774.subject: Chemistry
107774.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): $\text{B}_2$ molecule is paramagnetic, whereas $\text{C}_2$ molecule is diamagnetic.
Reason (R): In $\text{B}_2$ and $\text{C}_2$ molecules, the $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi 2p_y$ molecular orbitals are lower in energy than the $\sigma 2p_z$ molecular orbital.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
107774.sol:
Assertion is correct: According to Molecular Orbital Theory, the electronic configuration of $\text{B}_2$ (10 $e^-$) is $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^{*} 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^{*} 2s^2 \pi 2p_x^1 = \pi 2p_y^1$. It has two unpaired electrons, making it paramagnetic. The configuration of $\text{C}_2$ (12 $e^-$) is $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^{*} 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^{*} 2s^2 \pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2$. All electrons are paired, making it diamagnetic.

Reason is correct: For homonuclear diatomic molecules up to 14 electrons (like $\text{B}_2$ and $\text{C}_2$), due to $s-p$ mixing, the energy of the $\sigma 2p_z$ orbital is raised above the $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi 2p_y$ orbitals.

Reason explains Assertion: If the $\sigma 2p_z$ orbital were lower in energy than the $\pi 2p$ orbitals (as is the case in $\text{O}_2$), the two outermost electrons in $\text{B}_2$ would pair up in $\sigma 2p_z$, making it diamagnetic. Similarly, $\text{C}_2$ would have the configuration $\dots \sigma 2p_z^2 \pi 2p_x^1 = \pi 2p_y^1$, making it paramagnetic. The inversion of these energy levels is the exact reason why $\text{B}_2$ is paramagnetic and $\text{C}_2$ is diamagnetic. Thus, Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.

111933.subject: Chemistry
111933.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Halogens present in an organic compound cannot be detected by directly adding aqueous silver nitrate solution to the compound.
Reason (R): The elements in organic compounds are covalently bonded and do not furnish free ions in aqueous solution.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
111933.sol:
Organic compounds generally contain elements like halogens in covalently bonded states. Because they are covalent, they do not ionise in aqueous solutions to furnish free halide ions ($\text{X}^-$).

Aqueous silver nitrate ($\text{AgNO}_3$) reacts only with free halide ions to form a precipitate of silver halide ($\text{AgX}$). Since direct addition of $\text{AgNO}_3$ to the organic compound does not provide free halide ions, no precipitate is formed, and the halogens cannot be detected directly.

Therefore, both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

112655.subject: Chemistry
112655.text: An alkyl halide $\text{X}$ undergoes Wurtz reaction to yield an alkane $\text{Y}$ with the molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$. Alkane $\text{Y}$, upon photochemical monochlorination, yields exactly two structural isomers. Identify the starting alkyl halide $\text{X}$.
112655.sol:
The alkane $\text{Y}$ has the formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$. Since it yields exactly two structural isomers upon monochlorination, it must possess exactly two distinct sets of equivalent hydrogen atoms.

Let us evaluate the possible symmetrical hexanes formed via Wurtz reaction:
First, $n$-hexane (from 1-chloropropane) has three sets of equivalent hydrogens, yielding 3 monochloro isomers.
Second, 2,3-dimethylbutane (from 2-chloropropane) has 12 equivalent primary hydrogens and 2 equivalent tertiary hydrogens. It yields exactly 2 monochloro isomers.

Thus, alkane $\text{Y}$ is 2,3-dimethylbutane.

In the Wurtz reaction, two identical alkyl radicals couple to form the alkane. To obtain 2,3-dimethylbutane, the reacting alkyl halide must be an isopropyl halide.
Therefore, the starting alkyl halide $\text{X}$ is 2-chloropropane.

(Note: Chloroethane yields $n$-butane, which gives 2 isomers but has the formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$, not $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$. 1-Chloro-2-methylpropane yields 2,5-dimethylhexane, which gives 3 isomers.)

Answer: 2-Chloropropane

118080.subject: Chemistry
118080.text:
Which of the following gives cyanide when reacted with KCN
(A) Chloro benzene
(B) Allyl bromide
(C) Vinyl chloride
(D) Benzyl bromide
options: A, B and C are correct
118080.sol:
The reaction with KCN (potassium cyanide) involves an SN1 or SN2 nucleophilic substitution, where the cyanide ion (CN-) replaces a leaving group.
(B) Allyl bromide \(($\mathrm{CH}$2=$\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}$2 $\mathrm{Br})$\) and
(D) Benzyl bromide \(($\mathrm{C}$6 $\mathrm{H}$5-$\mathrm{CH}$2 $\mathrm{Br})$\)
both undergo SN1 or SN2 reactions with KCN to form the corresponding cyanides:
- Allyl bromide \( → \) Allyl cyanide (\($\mathrm{CH}$2=$\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}$2 $\mathrm{CN}$\))
- Benzyl bromide \( → \) Benzyl cyanide (C6H5-CH2CN)
(A) Chlorobenzene (C6H5Cl) does not react with KCN because the Cl - is not a good leaving group in an aromatic ring.
(C) Vinyl chloride \(($\mathrm{CH}$2=$\mathrm{CHCl})$\) does not undergo SN 1 or SN 2 reactions with KCN due to the stability of the vinyl carbocation and the presence of a chlorine atom bonded to a double bond, making it less reactive.
Therefore, only Allyl bromide and Benzyl bromide react with KCN to give cyanide compounds.
Hence, option (3) is correct.

118262.subject: Chemistry
118262.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Neopentyl chloride is highly reactive towards $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}2$ reaction because it is a primary alkyl halide.
Reason (R): The bulky tert-butyl group attached to the $\beta$-carbon in neopentyl chloride causes severe steric hindrance in the transition state.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
118262.sol:
Assertion (A) is false because despite being a primary ($1^{\circ}$) alkyl halide, neopentyl chloride (1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane) is practically unreactive towards $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}2$ mechanisms.

Reason (R) is true. In an $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}2$ reaction, the nucleophile attacks from the backside of the leaving group. In neopentyl chloride, the $\alpha$-carbon is attached to a highly bulky tert-butyl group at the $\beta$-position. This creates severe steric hindrance, blocking the approach of the nucleophile and making the transition state highly unstable (high activation energy).

Therefore, (A) is false but (R) is true.

Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true.

122016.subject: Botany
122016.text: The precursor to the seed habit is observed in some pteridophytes. In gymnosperms, which of the following characteristics is directly responsible for the definitive establishment of the seed habit?
options: The aggregation of sporophylls to form distinct and compact strobili or cones
The retention of the female gametophyte within the megasporangium on the parent sporophyte
The development of needle-like leaves with thick cuticles and sunken stomata
The dispersal of microspores by wind currents for pollination
122016.sol:
The seed habit is considered an important step in plant evolution. Its precursor is seen in heterosporous pteridophytes (like Selaginella and Salvinia) where the female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte for variable periods.

In gymnosperms, this evolutionary step is fully established. The female gametophyte does not have an independent free-living existence; it is permanently retained within the megasporangium (ovule) on the parent sporophyte. Fertilization and the subsequent development of the zygote into an embryo occur within this retained structure, which eventually transforms into a seed.

The formation of cones, leaf adaptations, and wind pollination are characteristic features of many gymnosperms but are not the direct morphological cause of the seed habit.

Answer: The retention of the female gametophyte within the megasporangium on the parent sporophyte

122193.subject: Botany
122193.text: What is the name of the mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development in some animals?
122193.sol: :Presence or absence of a cavity between the body wall and the gut wall is very important in classification. The body cavity, which is lined by mesoderm is called coelom. Animals possessing coelom are called coelomates, e.g., annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates. In some animals, the body cavity is not lined by mesoderm, instead, the mesoderm is present as scattered pouches in between the ectoderm and endoderm. Such a body cavity is called pseudocoelom and the animals possessing them are called pseudocoelomates, e.g., aschelminthes. The animals in which the body cavity is absent are called acoelomates, e.g., platyhelminthes Animals in which the cells are arranged in two embryonic layers, an external ectoderm and an internal endoderm, are called diploblastic animals, e.g., coelenterates Notochord is a mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development in some animals. Animals with notochord are called chordates and those animals which do not form this structure are called non-chordates, e.g., porifera to echinoderms.

124298.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The Golgi apparatus remains in close association with the endoplasmic reticulum.

Reason (R): Materials to be packaged in the form of vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus and move towards the maturing face.
